Synopsis:
    The Shanghai Futures Exchange is tightening trading controls on crude oil and low-sulfur fuel oil futures (October & November delivery) effective 14 September, capping intraday opening positions and raising price limit ranges to 16% and hedging margins to 17%. The move is a direct regulatory response to sharp oil price volatility driven by Middle East shipping route attacks, with oil already up 7%+ on the week.

Q01. Is the content's main message about EU energy, EU commodities, German power market prices, German energy economics?
Relevance: NO — The article focuses on Chinese exchange regulatory adjustments to oil futures, triggered by Middle East supply disruption fears. No direct reference to EU or German energy markets.

Q02. Is the content confirming already known information or reporting very new/uncertain risks?
Risk score: 55 — Middle East supply disruption risk is an ongoing known theme, but the specific escalation driving a 7%+ weekly oil price spike and prompting emergency exchange-level position limits adds a layer of uncertainty around the magnitude and duration of the disruption.

Q03. Is the content explicit about bullish impact on the German power futures market?
Explicit: NO — The article does not mention German power markets. However, a sustained oil price surge of this magnitude could indirectly support gas and power prices through cross-commodity sentiment and fuel-switching dynamics.
